metadata.title: For skilled comprehenders digital reading is a routine task, for unskilled comprehenders it is a problem

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012’s stratified sampling scheme, sampling schools within each country and then randomly sampling 35 students per school, and restricts the analytic sample to students who completed the PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment (CBA) with the relevant digital reading and complex problem solving clusters. All metric variables are standardized per country, and the authors estimate a path-analytic model using the R package bifie.survey. The nested design is handled via replicate weights, and students are weighted according to the final student weight (as stated in the sampling/weights section). Because the analysis is not ML prediction but survey-weighted path analysis with meta-analytic integration, the paper’s weighting strategy is essential for correct uncertainty under the clustered sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that WLEs were computed for digital reading, comprehension skill, and problem solving skill, but it does not describe any explicit missing-data handling procedure (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation) for the analytic sample. Given that the analytic sample is restricted to students completing specific CBA clusters and log-based navigation indicators, missingness could arise from incomplete cluster participation or incomplete log availability; however, the manuscript does not document how such cases were treated. This is therefore a reporting gap rather than a design-based reason for omitting missing-data details.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment (CBA) microdata. Included students who participated in the PISA 2012 CBA, completed one cluster of digital reading and one cluster of complex problem solving, and were assigned a minimum of one cluster print reading. The authors selected all such students across 32 countries (country-wise N between 218 and 1313). Students were then used in a path-analytic model with navigation indicators computed from log files (Precision and Adaptive processing) and WLEs computed for digital reading, comprehension skill, and problem solving skill.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment (CBA) — Digital reading (WLE) and navigation indicators; grade not specified
main_findings.performance_metrics: Meta-analytic main effects: comprehension skill → Precision b = 0.32 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [0.30; 0.34], I2 = 0.19, Q(31) = 39.88, p > 0.05; problem solving skill → Precision b = 0.27 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [0.24; 0.30], I2 = 0.57, Q(31) = 76.34, p < 0.001. Interaction (CS × PS) on Precision: b = −0.08 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [−0.11; −0.06], significant in 17/32 countries, I2 = 0.69, Q(31) = 102.49, p < 0.001.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 CBA the study leveraged comprehension skill and problem solving skill to predict Precision (navigation indicator), finding that both skills were positively associated with Precision and that their interaction was negative (compensatory pattern across comprehension levels). This indicates that improving complex problem solving may strengthen students’ ability to select relevant information in digital reading, especially for students with weaker comprehension, though the study is correlational and not causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment (CBA) — Digital reading (WLE) and navigation indicators; grade not specified
main_findings.performance_metrics: Meta-analytic main effects: comprehension skill → Adaptive processing b = 0.25 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [0.22; 0.28], I2 = 0.34, Q(31) = 40.03, p < 0.05; problem solving skill → Adaptive processing b = 0.15 (SE = 0.02), 95% CI [0.11; 0.18], I2 = 0.69, Q(31) = 112.50, p < 0.001. Interaction (CS × PS) on Adaptive processing: b = −0.02 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [−0.05; 0.00], not supported meta-analytically (significant in 5 countries), I2 = 0.53, Q(31) = 64.97, p < 0.001.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 CBA the study leveraged comprehension skill and problem solving skill to predict Adaptive processing (navigation indicator), finding positive main effects but no meta-analytic support for an interaction between the two skills. This indicates that both skills independently support adaptive time allocation during digital reading, suggesting that instructional interventions can target either comprehension or problem solving to improve adaptive processing, while compensatory effects may be more limited for time-on-task regulation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment (CBA) — Digital reading (WLE) and navigation indicators; grade not specified
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hypothesis 3 total effects on digital reading: problem solving skill b = 0.31 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [0.29; 0.33] over and above comprehension skill; comprehension skill b = 0.40 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [0.38; 0.42]. Interaction on digital reading: b = −0.05 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [−0.07; −0.03], significant in 11/32 countries, I2 = 0.45, Q(31) = 56.14, p < 0.01. Mediation via Precision: comprehension skill indirect effect b = 0.12 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [0.10; 0.13]; problem solving skill indirect effect b = 0.10 (SE = 0.01), 95% CI [0.09; 0.12]. Mediation via Adaptive processing: comprehension skill indirect effect b = 0.027 (SE = 0.004), 95% CI [0.02; 0.03]; problem solving skill indirect effect b = 0.015 (SE = 0.002), 95% CI [0.01; 0.02].
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 CBA the study leveraged comprehension skill and problem solving skill to predict digital reading (WLE), finding that both skills had positive direct/total associations and that their interaction was negative but only partially supported across countries. This indicates that strengthening complex problem solving alongside comprehension instruction may improve digital reading performance, with navigation behaviors (Precision and Adaptive processing) serving as mediating pathways, though causality cannot be inferred from the correlational design.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment (CBA) data across 32 countries (N = 13,080) focusing on digital reading navigation and performance. Students’ comprehension skill, problem solving skill, and digital reading were represented using author-computed WLEs, while navigation was operationalized from log files as Precision (relevant vs irrelevant page access) and Adaptive processing (time on relevant pages adjusted to item difficulty). Using a survey-weighted path-analytic approach with replicate weights and country-wise estimation integrated via random-effects meta-analysis, the authors report that comprehension and problem solving both positively predict Precision and Adaptive processing, with a compensatory interaction for Precision (negative CS×PS interaction) but not for Adaptive processing. Digital reading performance is predicted by both skills (e.g., problem solving b = 0.31; comprehension b = 0.40) and partially mediated through navigation indicators. Limitations include correlational inference and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling.
